At the lunch table in their Istanbul school, Wei leaned in. "Did you hear about Selin? Her mum came to school because she stole from the canteen."

Elif put down her sandwich. She had heard. Everyone had heard it three different ways.

"I don't want to talk about it," she said. "It's Selin's business."

Wei blinked. "Everyone's talking about it."

"Then I don't need to."

Wei looked around for someone else to tell, but the girl next to Elif just shrugged and went back to her book.

At the end of lunch, Selin walked past their table with her tray, eyes down. Nobody at Elif's table looked up or whispered. Selin's shoulders dropped a little, as if she'd been bracing for something that didn't come.

qa.a: That she stole from the canteen and her mum came to school.

qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and firm, not wanting to spread something that was Selin's business.

qa.a: Rumours need carriers; by refusing, Elif and the girl beside her gave the story nowhere to go at that table.

In the school library in Bhopal, Parul slid a note across to Seema. It said: Did you know Anjali's parents are getting divorced?? Pass it on!

Seema read it. Anjali sat two tables away, doing her homework with her head down.

Seema wrote underneath: I don't want to talk about this. It's her business. She folded the note and slid it back.

Parul frowned and whispered, "Why not? Everyone knows."

"Then they don't need me," Seema whispered back.

Parul held the note for a moment. Then she crumpled it and dropped it in the dustbin by the shelf.

Later, walking out, Seema passed Anjali's table and said, "Want to walk to the bus together?" Anjali looked surprised, then nodded.

qa.a: By refusing, she stopped the note, and Parul crumpled it instead of passing it on, so the rumour lost a carrier.

I sit behind Uma in Class 6, so I saw the whole thing on Thursday.

At break, Kanika came up to Uma's desk, all excited. "Uma, listen. Pinky got a zero in the test and cried in front of everyone in the parking lot. Don't tell anyone."

Uma didn't lean in. She said, "I don't want to talk about this. It's Pinky's business." Then she went back to her colouring.

Kanika looked at me instead. I didn't say anything, but I didn't ask for more either.

After break, I noticed Kanika didn't go to the next desk. She just sat down. The story stopped right there, as far as I know.

I felt a bit ashamed that I hadn't said it first.

— Simran

"I've heard some stories going around," she said. "I'm not going to say whose. But I want to talk about how words travel, and how they can hurt someone who sits right beside you."

After class, Vidya Ma'am asked Nikita to help carry books to the staffroom. On the way she said quietly, "If you ever want to talk, my door is open. And the counsellor, Mrs D'Souza, is kind."

Nikita nodded. The next day, when Rhea whispered something at lunch, Nikita said calmly, "That isn't true." Her voice didn't shake as much as she'd expected.

Shreya has been absent Monday and Tuesday. When she came today, she sat alone at the back and kept her dupatta pulled close. During break, two boys whistled as she passed; several girls whispered and looked away.

It's been two months since the rumour about me and the stolen phone, and I finally feel like myself again.

The school handled it. The girl who started it had to meet the principal with her parents, and she was suspended for a week. There was a whole assembly about how forwarding a message is a choice, and that choice has harm attached. Some people who'd forwarded it came up to me afterwards and said sorry. Not all of them.

What I remember most isn't the punishment, though. It's Santosh. On the worst day, when I was crying in the corridor, he stood next to me and told people to move on. He walked me to the counsellor's room. He sat with me at lunch for two weeks when no one else would.

We were just classmates before. Now he's the person I call first.

— Elizabeth

Six weeks ago Afreen came to me after a false rumour about her spread through the Class 9 chats. She was barely eating and had missed four days of school.

Since then, the school has acted. The student who started it met the principal with parents and faced consequences under our code. The class held a session on forwarding: every forward is a decision that can hurt someone. Two students came to apologise to Afreen in person.

She will check in with me monthly. I am closing weekly sessions.

Rashmi, her mother tells me, is the youngest of four, and her older sisters decide everything for her. This week she has started standing close to the tallest girls at recess, laughing loudly at their jokes.

At the government school in the village near Ambala, Sahil was the one everyone laughed with. But at home, his three older cousins bossed him around and teased him every evening, and nobody listened when he complained.

At recess he watched Mohit, a thin boy from the next village who ate his roti alone under the neem tree and never raised his voice.

Mohit wouldn't fight back. Sahil could tell.

The next day Sahil walked past and flicked Mohit's steel tiffin lid off. It clanged on the ground. The boys around Sahil laughed and looked at him as if he were a hero.

Mohit quietly picked it up.

Sahil laughed too, but somewhere under the laughing he felt like his cousins.

qa.q: Where did Mohit eat his roti alone?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when the boys looked at him like a hero?
qa.a: He felt powerful and admired, but also uneasy, feeling like his cousins.

qa.q: What could a teacher do after noticing this?
qa.a: Talk to Sahil calmly about what is going on for him and why he picked Mohit, stop the behaviour, and check on Mohit.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel picking up the tiffin lid?
qa.a: He probably feels humiliated and alone, not understanding why he was picked.

grounding: Sahil, powerless at home, notices a quiet classmate who won't fight back and targets him for admiration, not because of anything Mohit did.

The school bus was stuck behind a wedding procession for half an hour, and Varun was bored.

He looked at Neelam two seats ahead, the girl who stammered when she read aloud. He'd called her "Ne-Ne-Neelam" once last week, just to see. A few boys had laughed. Nobody had said anything.

Today he said it again, louder. Three boys laughed this time. Neelam stared out of the window.

Varun watched her ears go red. He watched the boys watching him. Nobody told him to stop. The driver had the radio on.

Then he reached over and took her water bottle and passed it to the back seat. More laughter.

Varun leaned back, grinning. It was easy. It worked. He was already thinking about what he could do tomorrow.

qa.q: What was the school bus stuck behind?
qa.a: A wedding procession.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when the boys laughed and nobody stopped him?
qa.a: He felt pleased and powerful, learning that the cruelty was rewarded with attention.

qa.q: What could have stopped this from growing?
qa.a: A classmate saying "stop", or the driver or a teacher stepping in, so Varun learned the cruelty did not pay; Neelam telling an adult that day would also help.

qa.q: What is it like for Neelam with her ears going red?
qa.a: She feels humiliated and helpless, staring out of the window while others laugh.

grounding: Varun tests Neelam with a nickname and taking her bottle, watching for reaction and audience, and learns from the laughter that cruelty pays.

In the colony park after school, Gautam noticed that Chetan always sat on the same bench with his comic.

On Monday, Gautam called him "Chashmish" because of his thick glasses. Two boys snickered. Chetan pushed his glasses up and kept reading.

On Tuesday, Gautam nudged him off the end of the bench "by accident." A few more laughed.

Gautam felt taller than he had in weeks.

That night he planned Thursday. Something bigger.
